title: Fairness or Fallacy? Mapping the Landscape of AI Bias in Disease Detection
authors: Ghulam Mudassir, Hameed Ullah Khan, Ahmad Sami Al-Shamayleh, Muhammad Faizan Khan, Muhammad Muqtasid, Moamin Abughazala
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has several transformative effects on healthcare, like to facilitate clinicians in disease detection and to manage patient care with enhanced precision. Due to the increasing complexity of medical data and the growing volume of diagnostic images, the substantial computational power needed to process such information creates both opportunities and challenges. To accomplish this objective, numerous methodologies have been proposed to integrate AI into disease detection systems. All these methodologies consider different aspects of clinical diagnosis, considering key parameters such as the type of AI model employed, the nature of input data, and the population demographics being analysed. In this paper, we review different state-of-the-art techniques which have been proposed for various areas of disease detection, specifically focusing on bias identification and mitigation. The proposed solutions are distinguished based on the type of input data they utilize, the architecture of model, and type of bias (algorithmic bias, demographic bias, model bias, and deployment bias). The time frame chosen to filter out relevant studies is between 2015 and 2026. Eventually, we review 23 related articles out of 64,389 analyzed from seven different digital libraries. The obtained results guide us to reach a conclusion with respect to state-of-the-art selected studies. Furthermore, these results reveal significant research gaps that can assist researchers in addressing AI-related bias in medical diagnosis. By prioritizing explainability, data diversity, and fairness in algorithmic design, as well as equitable access for affected patient populations, they can utilize available healthcare resources more effectively.

infographic.key_insight: This review maps bias in AI disease detection and highlights data diversity, explainability, and fairness-aware design as priorities for more equitable systems.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Bias in diagnostic AI may undermine equitable performance across patient populations, making demographic evaluation and deployment safeguards important.
method: Reviewed disease-detection AI literature within a stated 2015–2026 search window.
Analyzed approaches by input data, model architecture, and bias type.
Examined algorithmic, demographic, model, and deployment bias and mitigation strategies.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 23 included articles from 64,389 records analyzed across seven digital libraries, without quantitative estimates of mitigation effectiveness.
infographic.watch_item: The review identifies research priorities but does not establish that any mitigation strategy improves diagnostic fairness in clinical deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Fairness or Fallacy? Mapping the Landscape of AI Bias in Disease Detection

title: From Clinical Risk Prediction to Operational Decisions: An Uncertainty-Aware Framework for ICU Staffing
authors: Jiayan Yang, Ad Feelders, Arno Siebes
abstract: Advances in electronic health records (EHR) and large-scale critical care databases have enabled the development of machine learning models for the early detection of patient deterioration. While these models often achieve strong predictive performance for outcomes such as sepsis and mortality, most studies evaluate them purely on discrimination metrics. This leaves a critical gap: how to systematically translate probabilistic clinical risk estimates into downstream operational decisions under real-world constraints, such as shift rigidity and hiring delays. This study proposes an uncertainty-aware anticipatory staffing framework that bridges short-term patient risk prediction and staff planning without altering the upstream predictive model. Instead of relying on naive deterministic aggregation or fixed safety buffers, the framework explicitly models dynamic predictive uncertainty and evaluates extreme shortage exposure using Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR). These aggregated, risk-calibrated demand signals are then embedded into an hourly rolling-horizon scheduling policy to generate delay-constrained staffing decisions. Evaluated on realistic trajectories from the MIMIC-IV database, the proposed framework demonstrates a favorable cost-shortage trade-off compared to deterministic and purely reactive baselines. Pareto frontier analysis illustrates how uncertainty-aware demand construction changes resource allocation under varying safety preferences, while stress testing confirms the framework's operational robustness even when subjected to systematic predictive bias in the form of calibration drift. By formalizing this translation layer, this work provides a principled, transparent pathway for safely integrating probabilistic AI outputs into high-stakes healthcare operational systems.

infographic.key_insight: An uncertainty-aware framework translates predicted patient deterioration risk into ICU staffing plans that balance staffing costs against severe shortage exposure.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could support ICU workforce planning while accounting for hiring delays and inflexible shifts, without changing the underlying prediction model.
method: Aggregate patient risk predictions while explicitly modeling dynamic predictive uncertainty.
Use Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) to quantify extreme shortage exposure.
Embed risk-calibrated demand signals in hourly rolling-horizon staffing decisions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation on realistic MIMIC-IV trajectories showed a favorable cost–shortage trade-off versus deterministic and reactive baselines, with Pareto analysis and calibration-drift stress testing.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports trajectory-based evaluation rather than prospective deployment, so real-world staffing feasibility and patient-care effects remain unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: From Clinical Risk Prediction to Operational Decisions: An Uncertainty-Aware Framework for ICU Staffing

title: Temporal Evidence Allocation For Longitudinal Clinical Retrieval: A Position And Technical Report
authors: Soumya Ranjan Sahoo, Divya Bharti, Sanand Sasidharan
abstract: Electronic health records are written to support care, not retrieval. Across years of oncology notes, the primary diagnosis is restated in report after report, while the events that shape a patient's course, such as a recurrence or a change in therapy, may be recorded only once. A retriever that ranks passages by similarity to the query keeps returning the repeated material and can miss these transitions, that is, it exhibits temporal redundancy across historical narratives. We argue that longitudinal clinical retrieval should be treated as allocating a limited evidence budget across time, not just ranking by relevance. We separate the task into three objectives: temporal evidence allocation, candidate reconstruction, and clinical validation. In Study A (13 clinical queries over 20 patient records, with two-stage reconstruction), the Temporal-15 configuration reaches a milestone slot recall of 0.538, compared with 0.388 for the Global-50 baseline. However, it also retrieves far more evidence (496 versus 50 indexed units per query), so the gain cannot be credited to allocation alone. When evidence is held fixed, removing prompted precedence rules raises schema-order reversals from 0.010 to 0.080. A five-patient, single-query pilot with fixed budgets finds that wider temporal coverage does not reliably yield more dated milestones. Together, these results suggest that how much a record says about a period is a poor guide to how useful that period is as evidence. Because no expert reference timelines are available, our measurements describe retrieval behavior rather than clinical accuracy. This position and technical report presents the retrieval analysis behind the Onco-CONSTRUE framework and sets out a research agenda for budget-constrained longitudinal clinical retrieval.

infographic.key_insight: Longitudinal clinical retrieval should allocate limited evidence across time, rather than repeatedly retrieve similar passages that may miss important transitions.
infographic.clinical_relevance: For oncology record review, time-aware retrieval may help surface sparsely documented recurrences or therapy changes, but clinical accuracy remains unvalidated.
method: Separate temporal evidence allocation, candidate reconstruction, and clinical validation.
Compare Temporal-15 with Global-50 retrieval using two-stage reconstruction.
Test prompted precedence rules and explore temporal coverage under fixed evidence budgets.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 13 queries over 20 patient records, Temporal-15 achieved milestone slot recall of 0.538 versus 0.388 for Global-50, but retrieved 496 versus 50 indexed units per query.
infographic.watch_item: Unequal evidence budgets confound the main comparison, and without expert reference timelines, the results measure retrieval behavior—not clinical accuracy.
infographic.paper_title: Temporal Evidence Allocation For Longitudinal Clinical Retrieval: A Position And Technical Report

title: A general-purpose System One decision model for clinical records
authors: Andrew Zhang, Trinh T. L. Vuong, Sophia J. Wagner, Dongmin Bang, Tong Ding, Yuchang Su
abstract: Clinical care, health-system operations and biomedical discovery depend on extracting reliable answers from patient records, yet applying diverse clinical questions across entire populations remains computationally expensive. Here we present Clinical System One (CS1), a 4-billion-parameter decision model for fast, typed judgments from clinical records, along with two agentic harnesses in which CS1 works together with a generalist language model. CS1-4B is trained on 12.4 million questions and answers from 3.6 million patients across a multi-hospital health system, combining structured-data keys, observed outcomes and language-model supervision across clinical notes, diagnostic reports and patient timelines. It answers multiple typed questions in a single forward pass without task-specific retraining, and each answer carries a probability that can route uncertain cases to human review. On 963,408 held-out patients, CS1-4B outperformed open decision models up to 27 billion parameters on 13 of 14 tasks scored independently of its training teacher. Across 21 external data sets, its aggregate performance approached that of the strongest tested 27-billion-parameter model, with 6.4-fold faster inference in a matched workload. Integrating CS1-4B with a language model agent produced cited answers over complete multi-year patient histories and screened a patient population against the eligibility criteria of 17 registered clinical trials, placing four times as many judged-eligible patients among its top 20 candidates as keyword search while using 690-fold fewer language-model tokens than a language model reading every record. These findings support a division of labour in clinical AI, with small decision models performing repeated record reading and generative models formulating questions and synthesizing evidence.

infographic.key_insight: A compact clinical decision model can handle repeated record-reading tasks efficiently, while a generalist language model formulates questions and synthesizes evidence.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This approach could support patient-record review and trial eligibility screening, with answer probabilities helping route uncertain cases to human review.
method: Trained a 4-billion-parameter model on 12.4 million question–answer pairs from 3.6 million patients.
Answered multiple typed questions in one forward pass without task-specific retraining.
Paired the model with language-model agents for cited longitudinal summaries and trial screening.
infographic.evidence_signal: On 963,408 held-out patients, CS1-4B outperformed open decision models up to 27B on 13 of 14 independently scored tasks; across 21 external datasets, aggregate performance approached the strongest tested 27B model with 6.4× faster inference in a matched workload.
infographic.watch_item: Benchmark performance does not establish clinical safety; deployment needs prospective validation, calibrated uncertainty estimates and human oversight.
infographic.paper_title: A general-purpose System One decision model for clinical records

title: Africa-Papers: A 10-Billion-Token Multi-Domain Academic Corpus for African Foundation Language Models
authors: Mich-Seth Owusu
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) depend fundamentally on the diversity, depth, and factual rigor of their pre-training corpora. However, contemporary foundational pre-training datasets (such as The Pile, S2ORC, and Dolma) exhibit a severe structural omission: African scientific, medical, legal, and agricultural scholarship constitutes less than 0.5% of global pre-training tokens. Consequently, state-of-the-art models suffer from systematic failure modes when reasoning about tropical epidemiology, localized smallholder agro-ecologies, regional economic governance, and indigenous linguistic structures. To resolve this representation deficit and advance African intellectual sovereignty in artificial intelligence, we introduce Africa-Papers, the largest curated multi-domain Pan-African academic pre-training corpus to date. Comprising over 844,807 full-text papers spanning 10.15 billion tokens across 879 Parquet shards, Africa-Papers unifies four primary scientific streams: (1) continental peer-reviewed journals indexed in DOAJ across 31 African nations, (2) the CGIAR CGSpace agricultural repository, (3) African-authored and African-focused STEM/AI preprints on arXiv, and (4) open-access international publications by scholars affiliated with African institutions indexed via OpenAlex. The entire corpus is processed into layout-aware, clean Markdown preserving section hierarchies, mathematical equations, and tabular data, accompanied by exact BPE token counts and a standardized 8-domain taxonomy. We release Africa-Papers openly on the Hugging Face Hub under the AfriSpeech organization to accelerate continual pre-training and domain evaluation for foundation models globally.

infographic.key_insight: Africa-Papers introduces an open, 10.15-billion-token academic corpus designed to improve African representation in foundation-model training.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Its African medical scholarship may support research on locally relevant clinical language models, but clinical benefits are not demonstrated in the abstract.
method: Combines African journals, CGIAR CGSpace, African-focused arXiv preprints, and OpenAlex-indexed publications.
Converts full texts into layout-aware Markdown preserving sections, equations, and tables.
Adds exact BPE token counts and a standardized eight-domain taxonomy.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 844,807 full-text papers across 879 Parquet shards, with the journal stream spanning 31 African nations, but no downstream model or clinical evaluation.
infographic.watch_item: Corpus scale alone does not establish balanced coverage or clinical reliability; downstream performance and safety require evaluation.
infographic.paper_title: Africa-Papers: A 10-Billion-Token Multi-Domain Academic Corpus for African Foundation Language Models

title: Discrete Neural Interlingua for Ontology-Agnostic EHR Modeling
authors: Tong Ding, Caiwei Tian, Dongmin Bang, Ming Y. Lu, Sophia J. Wagner, Andrew Zhang
abstract: EHR foundation models promise scalable clinical prediction across health systems, yet their deployment is constrained by a tokenization bottleneck. The same clinical concept can appear as different ontology codes, local identifiers, synonyms, or free-text descriptions, which standard EHR tokenizers treat as unrelated symbols. A model trained on MIMIC-III with a closed-vocabulary tokenizer can use only 13% of eICU events. We introduce MEDIATOR, a discrete ontology-agnostic tokenizer that maps any clinical concept expressed as text into a shared vector-quantized codebook, turning EHR harmonization into open-vocabulary tokenization without manual mappings or a fixed vocabulary. Trained with synonym supervision and guided by enriched concept descriptions, code co-occurrence, and relation graphs, MEDIATOR collapses equivalent expressions while organizing distinct concepts in a medically meaningful discrete space. Used as the token interface of an EHR Transformer, MEDIATOR improves mean AUPRC over the strongest prior tokenizer by 4.0 points (8% relative) on 20 MIMIC-III tasks and by 8.6 points (29% relative) in zero-shot transfer to 14 eICU tasks, where it uses all events. The transfer gain combines coverage and representation, as MEDIATOR remains the best tokenizer under identical inputs (+1.0 and +1.9 points on operational and subcohort-mortality tasks). Same-encoder controls show that the text encoder drives in-domain accuracy, while the learned objectives of MEDIATOR drive transfer robustness and entity-linking quality. MEDIATOR also enables transferable attribution across hospitals.

infographic.key_insight: MEDIATOR maps clinical text into shared discrete tokens, improving EHR prediction across hospitals without manual ontology mappings or a fixed vocabulary.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could help prediction models reuse differently coded EHR data across health systems, but clinical utility remains unestablished.
method: Maps text-described clinical concepts into a shared vector-quantized codebook.
Learns from synonyms, enriched descriptions, code co-occurrence, and relation graphs.
Supplies ontology-agnostic tokens to an EHR Transformer.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 20 MIMIC-III tasks and zero-shot transfer to 14 eICU tasks, MEDIATOR improved mean AUPRC over the strongest prior tokenizer by 4.0 and 8.6 points, respectively, while using all eICU events.
infographic.watch_item: Transfer gains reflect both broader event coverage and better representations; prospective clinical validation is not reported in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Discrete Neural Interlingua for Ontology-Agnostic EHR Modeling

title: Unified Multiparadigm Fusion Intelligence for Rare Disease Diagnosis
authors: Jian Yang, Peiling Liu, Songda Li, Yu Cao, Yuqing Feng, Lan Yu
abstract: Rare diseases (RDs) affect an estimated 300 million people globally, leaving patients to navigate a protracted diagnostic odyssey constrained by clinical scarcity and fragmented medical knowledge. Artificial intelligence (AI) has progressively advanced RD diagnostics, from symbolic methods and deep learning to large language model (LLM)-based systems. However, each paradigm carries structural limitations: symbolic methods are bounded by knowledge completeness, neural models sacrifice interpretability, and LLM-based systems are vulnerable to evaluation biases like data leakage. In this study, we introduce FusionRare, a unified multiparadigm fusion framework integrating knowledge-driven symbolic reasoning, deep-learning pattern recognition, case-based patient retrieval, and LLM-based heuristic inference via statistical meta-aggregation and knowledge-enhanced agentic reflection. Evaluated on 2,528 strictly isolated clinical cases, FusionRare achieves state-of-the-art RD prioritization, attaining a macro-averaged Recall @1 of 51% for phenotype-only diagnosis and 79% for phenotype-genotype joint analysis. These results represent decisive advantages over the advanced agentic system DeepRare, frontier LLMs including GPT 5.5, and specialized tools like PhenoBrain and LIRICAL under stringent anti-leakage protocols. A randomized, crossover clinician-AI validation demonstrated that FusionRare elevates the true diagnostic rank in 45% of decisions, improves physician confidence in 62%, and reduces time to diagnosis by 21%. These findings indicate that reconciling these orthogonal AI paradigms significantly enhances diagnostic capabilities, bridging the gap between computational benchmarks and actionable clinical reliability. More broadly, this work provides a replicable framework for deploying trustworthy diagnostic AI across complex, high-stakes, and underserved medical domains.

infographic.key_insight: FusionRare combines complementary AI approaches and reports macro-averaged Recall@1 of 51% using phenotypes alone and 79% using phenotypes plus genotypes for rare-disease prioritization.
infographic.clinical_relevance: In a clinician-AI study, FusionRare improved the true diagnosis’s rank in 45% of decisions, increased physician confidence in 62%, and reduced time to diagnosis by 21%.
method: Combines symbolic reasoning, deep-learning pattern recognition, patient-case retrieval, and LLM inference.
Integrates outputs through statistical meta-aggregation and knowledge-enhanced agentic reflection.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports evaluation on 2,528 strictly isolated clinical cases under anti-leakage protocols, plus randomized crossover clinician-AI validation.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish prospective real-world diagnostic accuracy or patient outcomes; broader clinical validation remains important.
infographic.paper_title: Unified Multiparadigm Fusion Intelligence for Rare Disease Diagnosis

title: 3D Diffusion Models for Medical Imaging
authors: Frank-Peter Schilling, Daniel Barco, Philipp Denzel, Marc Stadelmann
abstract: Generative deep learning methods such as Variational Autoencoders, Generative Adversarial Networks or Diffusion Models have achieved remarkable results in image synthesis. In particular, Diffusion Models have demonstrated superior image fidelity and sample diversity compared to other approaches on standard benchmarks, while also offering more flexible training dynamics as evidenced both in natural image domains and in medical applications. In medical imaging including Computed Tomography, Magnetic Resonance Imaging or Positron Emission Tomography, such models have various important use-cases including data augmentation, domain transfer, image reconstruction, inpainting, image augmentation and artifact correction. Further, generated images can be conditioned on patient characteristics, medical reports, segmentation masks or other images. Specific challenges arise due to the 3D volumetric nature of medical images, which translate to substantial demands in terms of memory, compute, and training data. This article provides a comparative overview of 3D Diffusion Models which have been developed for medical images, with a focus on current performance, limitations, and an outlook for future work.

infographic.key_insight: This review compares 3D diffusion models for medical imaging, highlighting their potential for volumetric image generation and enhancement alongside substantial resource demands.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Potential applications across CT, MRI, and PET include data augmentation, reconstruction, inpainting, domain transfer, and artifact correction.
method: Reviews diffusion models developed for 3D medical images.
Examines conditioning on patient characteristics, reports, segmentation masks, or other images.
Compares current performance, limitations, and future directions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes a comparative overview but provides no dataset sizes, quantitative evaluation results, or clinical validation outcomes.
infographic.watch_item: High memory, compute, and training-data requirements may limit implementation of 3D models.
infographic.paper_title: 3D Diffusion Models for Medical Imaging

title: Brain2Vec: A Self-Supervised 3D Foundation Model for Structural Brain MRI
authors: Spiros Maggioros, Guray Erus, Gareth Harman, George Aidinis, Alexander Getka, Aristeidis Sotiras
abstract: Deep learning models have become essential tools in medical imaging, yet training them end-to-end for diverse tasks remains challenging due to limited labeled data and computational constraints. To address this, we introduce Brain2Vec, a foundation model pre-trained on 74,425 T1-weighted Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) scans pooled from multiple studies. Brain2Vec can serve both as a weight initialization backbone for fine-tuning downstream tasks and as a standalone feature extractor. We evaluated Brain2Vec in three tasks: downstream predictive performance, convergence speed, and embedding quality. Using Brain2Vec's pretrained weights as initialization and fine-tuning on labeled data for a brain age prediction task, results demonstrate improved final accuracy and faster convergence compared to random initialization. Additionally, its frozen embeddings outperform anatomically defined volumetric features on four of five downstream classification tasks and perform competitively with a state-of-the-art foundation model pre-trained on substantially more data. Lastly, we show that Brain2Vec encodes information primarily from a spatially localized and neuroanatomically meaningful set of brain regions, and that manipulating a subset of latent features produces monotonic, region-specific effects on the reconstructed anatomy. Brain2Vec code and trained models are available as an open-source package on https://github.com/CBICA/Brain2Vec. Users can apply Brain2Vec locally by installing the package, or directly through the NiChart cloud platform https://cloud.neuroimagingchart.com, where Brain2Vec features can be derived without requiring local installation or specialized infrastructure.

infographic.key_insight: Brain2Vec learns reusable 3D brain MRI representations that improve brain-age prediction and support classification with frozen features.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The model could support research on structural brain MRI by reducing task-specific training demands, but clinical utility is not established in the abstract.
method: Self-supervised pretraining on 74,425 T1-weighted brain MRI scans pooled across studies.
Use pretrained weights for downstream fine-tuning or extract features with the model frozen.
Probe spatial localization and latent-feature effects on reconstructed anatomy.
infographic.evidence_signal: Pretrained initialization improved brain-age accuracy and convergence versus random initialization; frozen embeddings outperformed anatomical volumetric features on four of five classification tasks.
infographic.watch_item: Performance across clinical sites, scanners, and patient populations requires further validation before clinical use.
infographic.paper_title: Brain2Vec: A Self-Supervised 3D Foundation Model for Structural Brain MRI

title: CODA: Cohort- and Drift-aware Foundation Model for Multimodal Clinical Reasoning
authors: Changshuo Liu, Jiaqi Zhu, Wenqiao Zhang, Xiaokui Xiao, Beng Chin Ooi
abstract: Recent advances in multimodal foundation models have demonstrated strong performance across diverse clinical tasks. However, existing approaches predominantly operate at the individual sample level and fail to model the interplay between population-level cohort patterns and patient-specific variation that underlie real-world clinical reasoning. In practice, clinicians routinely reason through patient cohorts sharing similar demographic, physiological, or pathological characteristics, while accounting for patient-specific deviations from the group prototype. Motivated by this gap, we propose CODA, a cohort- and drift-aware foundation model for multimodal clinical reasoning. CODA explicitly integrates cohort structure into the modeling pipeline through two complementary mechanisms: cohort-aware population stratification and drift-aware individual adaptation. In particular, we leverage reinforcement learning to discover clinically meaningful patient cohorts, and further model each patient's deviation from cohort prototypes as a structured drift signal encoding fine-grained individual heterogeneity. These cohort- and drift-aware representations are incorporated into the foundation model to enable reasoning that is simultaneously informed by population-level patterns and sensitive to individual-level variation. Extensive experiments on real-world electronic health record (EHR) benchmarks demonstrate that CODA achieves consistent effectiveness and strong generalizability across diverse clinical tasks, including closed-QA, open-QA, and report generation.

infographic.key_insight: CODA combines patient-cohort patterns with individual deviations to support multimodal clinical reasoning.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach aims to contextualize patient-specific information within similar patient groups for clinical question answering and report generation.
method: Uses reinforcement learning to discover clinically meaningful patient cohorts.
Represents each patient’s deviation from a cohort prototype as a structured drift signal.
Integrates cohort and drift representations into a multimodal foundation model.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports consistent effectiveness and strong generalizability on real-world EHR benchmarks for closed-QA, open-QA, and report generation, without numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Benchmark performance does not establish clinical safety or utility; prospective validation is needed before clinical use.
infographic.paper_title: CODA: Cohort- and Drift-aware Foundation Model for Multimodal Clinical Reasoning

title: A Multi-Agent Framework for Automated Machine Learning with Evidence-based Planning for Medical Image Analysis
authors: Yiqing Shen, Mathias Unberath
abstract: Deep learning has become the default tool for medical image analysis, driven by the open-source movement. However, achieving the best performance on a given task remains difficult, with architecture selection and hyperparameter optimization (HPO) still considered "more of an art than a science". Automated machine learning (AutoML) automates parts of model training, yet helps little in medical imaging: general-purpose approaches lack medical architectures and preprocessing, and medical-focused ones demand engineering expertise and remain confined to narrow tasks such as 3D segmentation. We introduce MedicalMLOmni, a multi-agent AutoML framework that automates model training for diverse single- and multi-modal medical tasks through a natural language interface. Specifically, MedicalMLOmni performs evidence-based planning by retrieving published results to guide model selection and configuration, and employs parallel HPO where multiple agents explore adjustment strategies concurrently. MedicalMLOmni achieves the best score on 19 of 20 benchmarks; PMC-VQA is the exception, where a vision-language model with broader pre-training leads. Backbone-matched controls attribute the gains to the framework, not the backbone. By removing coding requirements, MedicalMLOmni lowers the barrier for domain experts with rich datasets but limited engineering expertise.

infographic.key_insight: MedicalMLOmni uses multiple AI agents and published evidence to automate medical imaging model development, reporting the best score on 19 of 20 benchmarks.
infographic.clinical_relevance: A natural language interface could help medical researchers with limited engineering expertise develop imaging models, but benchmark results do not establish clinical readiness.
method: Retrieve published results to guide model selection and configuration.
Run multiple agents in parallel to explore hyperparameter adjustments.
Automate training for diverse single- and multimodal medical tasks.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports top scores on 19 of 20 benchmarks and backbone-matched controls attributing gains to the framework; PMC-VQA favored a vision-language model with broader pretraining.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not report prospective clinical validation, leaving real-world reliability and generalizability uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: A Multi-Agent Framework for Automated Machine Learning with Evidence-based Planning for Medical Image Analysis

title: Can Language Models Get "Aphasia" From Neuronal Ablation?
authors: Pratik Worah, Randall Bateman
abstract: Progressive neuronal loss is the hallmark of neurodegenerative disease, yet how loss of neurons shapes the pattern of cognitive decline remains poorly understood. Here we systematically ablate neurons (computational units) in language models spanning recurrent long short-term memory (LSTM) and Transformer architectures and apply limited fine-tuning as a simple proxy for compensatory plasticity. With whole-unit ablation, LSTMs degrade gradually with syntactic and semantic faculties declining in parallel across mild-to-moderate damage. By contrast, Transformers exhibit late threshold-like collapse under feedforward multi-layer perceptron (MLP) ablation and smoother sigmoid-like decline under attention-head ablation. Qualitatively, MLP-ablated models continue to make within-category semantic substitutions (semantic paraphasias) alongside rising non-responses, paralleling Wernicke-type aphasia, while attention-head ablation produces a trend toward loss of semantic specificity similar to the semantic variant of primary progressive aphasia (svPPA). These findings indicate that feedforward and attentional pathways have functionally distinct failure modes, suggesting that architecture-dependent failure profiles may offer new computational perspectives on aphasic syndromes and neurodegenerative diseases as an in silico model. Notably, early accuracy retention under Transformer attention-head ablation qualitatively parallels pre-symptomatic reserve before the 40--60% neuronal loss reported by Gomez-Isla et al. (1996) when clinical symptoms emerge in Alzheimer's disease, whereas the steadier LSTM decline parallels the symptomatic progression described by DeKosky and Scheff (1990) and Terry et al. (1991).

infographic.key_insight: Ablating computational units produces architecture-dependent language failures, with some Transformer errors qualitatively resembling aphasic language patterns.
infographic.clinical_relevance: These simulations may help generate hypotheses about language decline in neurodegeneration, but do not establish biological mechanisms or clinical utility.
method: Systematically ablate units in LSTM and Transformer language models.
Compare Transformer feedforward MLP and attention-head ablation.
Apply limited fine-tuning as a proxy for compensatory plasticity.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports gradual LSTM decline, late threshold-like collapse with Transformer MLP ablation, and smoother sigmoid-like decline with attention-head ablation, without quantitative results or patient validation.
infographic.watch_item: Computational unit ablation and limited fine-tuning are simplified proxies for neuronal loss and plasticity; resemblance to aphasia does not demonstrate equivalent pathology.
infographic.paper_title: Can Language Models Get "Aphasia" From Neuronal Ablation?

title: DeliMF: Gated Cross-Attention Fusion of Structured Time Series and Clinical Text for Early Intensive Care Delirium Prediction
authors: Yibo Yang, Zerui Huang, Haomiao Yang, Zixia Wang
abstract: Delirium affects a large fraction of intensive care unit (ICU) patients and foreshadows longer stays, lasting cognitive decline, and higher mortality. Flagging the patients who will become delirious within the first day of admission would give clinicians a window to intervene. Yet state-of-the-art predictors rely only on the structured electronic health record (EHR) of vital signs, laboratory values, and medications, while overlooking the free-text clinical notes written in the same window, which carry information the numbers cannot encode. To this end, we present DeliMF, a multimodal framework that fuses the structured time series with clinical text. It encodes the structured signals with a temporal Transformer and the time-stamped radiology reports with a clinical text encoder, and fuses the two through a gated cross-attention module. The gate learns a per-patient weight on the text; when a patient has no note the gate closes and DeliMF reduces to its structured-only form, giving robustness to missing text by construction. On an incident-only MIMIC-IV cohort, DeliMF improves significantly over the baselines, particularly on patients who carry clinical text, while losing nothing on those without. Ablation studies confirm the contribution of multimodal fusion and gated cross-attention, and a case study further shows that fusing clinical text with the structured stream recovers delirium cases that the structured data alone misses. We hope DeliMF encourages early ICU prediction to make fuller use of the overlooked clinical text and contributes to the early identification and timely intervention of delirium.

infographic.key_insight: DeliMF combines structured ICU data with clinical text to improve early delirium prediction while falling back to structured-only prediction when text is missing.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Earlier identification of patients at risk for delirium could support timely clinical assessment, though clinical benefit was not established in the abstract.
method: A temporal Transformer encodes structured EHR time series.
A clinical text encoder processes time-stamped radiology reports.
Gated cross-attention learns patient-specific text weights and closes the gate when notes are absent.
infographic.evidence_signal: On an incident-only MIMIC-IV cohort, the authors report significant gains over baselines, especially for patients with text, with no performance loss reported for those without; ablations support the fusion design.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no numerical performance estimates or external validation, leaving the size and generalizability of gains uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: DeliMF: Gated Cross-Attention Fusion of Structured Time Series and Clinical Text for Early Intensive Care Delirium Prediction

title: GAMF-Net: Grouped Availability-Aware Multimodal Fusion for Smartphone Skin Lesion Classification
authors: Yue Zhuo, Jingjia Yan, Fangyu Liu, Lingjun Liu, Zongjun Chen, Zhisheng Luo
abstract: Smartphone clinical images provide a low-cost data source for computer-aided skin lesion classification in resource-constrained settings, but images alone cannot fully capture patients' medical histories and lesion symptoms. To address the lack of structured organization among heterogeneous clinical variables, the ambiguity between observed and imputed values, and the risk that clinical information may interfere with visual evidence, we propose GAMF-Net, a grouped availability-aware multimodal fusion network. Ten clinical variables are divided into three semantic groups---demographics, history-related risk, and lesion presentation---and each group jointly encodes field values and field-level availability masks. The image branch produces the base classification logits, while each clinical group generates image-conditioned class-level residual evidence. Only available groups participate in availability-normalized equal-weight fusion; when all clinical information is unavailable, the model reduces exactly to the image-only pathway. We evaluate the method on PAD-UFES-20 under a patient-disjoint five-fold protocol with separate training, validation, and test partitions. GAMF-Net achieves an Accuracy of $74.17\pm2.85\%$, a balanced accuracy (BACC) of $70.11\pm2.11\%$, a Macro-F1 of $68.85\pm0.85\%$, and a Macro-AUROC of $93.42\pm1.20\%$, outperforming all image-only and multimodal baselines reimplemented under a unified protocol. Compared with the strongest baseline, MetaBlock, the corresponding improvements are 2.37, 2.59, 4.14, and 1.02 percentage points, respectively. Ablation results show that clinical information substantially improves class-balanced performance, constrained equal-weight fusion is more effective than dynamic fusion, and the lesion-presentation group provides the most informative clinical complement.

infographic.key_insight: GAMF-Net improves smartphone skin lesion classification by combining image predictions with grouped clinical information while explicitly tracking missing fields.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could support low-cost skin lesion assessment in resource-constrained settings, but clinical utility remains unproven.
method: Groups 10 clinical variables into demographics, history-related risk, and lesion presentation.
Encodes values and availability masks; each group adds image-conditioned evidence to image-based predictions.
Equally weights available groups and reverts exactly to image-only predictions when all clinical information is missing.
infographic.evidence_signal: On PAD-UFES-20 with patient-disjoint five-fold evaluation and separate training, validation, and test partitions, GAMF-Net achieved 74.17±2.85% accuracy and 70.11±2.11% balanced accuracy, exceeding the strongest reimplemented baseline by 2.37 and 2.59 percentage points, respectively.
infographic.watch_item: Evaluation was limited to one dataset; performance across external populations, smartphone devices, and real-world missing-data patterns remains uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: GAMF-Net: Grouped Availability-Aware Multimodal Fusion for Smartphone Skin Lesion Classification

title: IECG: Weakly-Supervised Interpretability-Enhancing Foundation Model for Electrocardiogram
authors: Huynh Dang Nguyen, Trong-Thang Pham, Anh-Thuan Do, Phuong-Nhi Dinh, Brijesh Patel, Ngan Le
abstract: Electrocardiography (ECG) is a cornerstone of cardiac diagnosis, yet most machine learning methods for ECG analysis lack interpretability, limiting their clinical adoption. We present IECG, a weakly-supervised ECG foundation model that jointly performs diagnostic classification and abnormality localization without requiring manual abnormal region annotations, overcoming a long-standing bottleneck in interpretable ECG learning. Central to IECG is a weakly-supervised attention strategy that explicitly incorporates clinical priors by deriving abnormality heatmap pseudo-labels from established ECG clinical knowledge. These pseudo-labels guide the model's CLS-token attention through a KL-divergence loss, encouraging it to focus on diagnostically relevant waveform regions. During pretraining, IECG is jointly optimized with clinically guided attention supervision, ECG-text contrastive alignment, and report captioning objectives, enabling it to learn rich multimodal representations while producing localized waveform evidence. By explicitly aggregating features from clinically guided attention regions, IECG grounds its diagnostic predictions in interpretable waveform evidence without sacrificing classification performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that IECG achieves state-of-the-art abnormal region localization while maintaining strong classification performance, advancing trustworthy foundation models for ECG analysis.

infographic.key_insight: IECG links ECG diagnostic predictions to localized waveform evidence without requiring manually annotated abnormal regions.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Highlighting waveform regions associated with predictions could make AI-assisted ECG interpretation easier to scrutinize, though clinical benefit is not established in the abstract.
method: Derives abnormality heatmap pseudo-labels from established ECG clinical knowledge.
Guides CLS-token attention with a KL-divergence loss alongside ECG–text alignment and report captioning objectives.
Aggregates features from attention-guided regions to support diagnostic classification.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports state-of-the-art abnormal-region localization and strong classification performance, but provides no dataset details or numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Reliance on clinical-prior-derived pseudo-labels warrants checking whether highlighted regions remain reliable across diverse ECG patterns and clinical settings.
infographic.paper_title: IECG: Weakly-Supervised Interpretability-Enhancing Foundation Model for Electrocardiogram

title: SCODEL: Shared Canonical Ontology Definitions for Food Entity Linking and Ontology-Grounded Recipe Knowledge Graphs
authors: Nuhu Ibrahim, Rishi Ravikumar, Ayuba Dauda, Fuqi Xu, Robert Stevens, Riza Batista-Navarro
abstract: Identifying recipe entities and linking them to ontology concepts is fundamental for semantic recipe understanding. However, food mentions in recipes are often ambiguous, context-dependent, and lexically diverse, making ontology entity linking (EL) challenging. We propose SCODEL, a streamlined, model-agnostic approach based on a central idea: contextual food mentions and ontology concepts that refer to the same entity should learn the same canonical ontology-oriented definition. SCODEL uses these shared definitions as a semantic normalisation layer, providing complementary semantic information to existing EL models without requiring a new linking architecture. We further introduce ReciLinkD, the first benchmark for contextual food ontology entity linking in recipes. Experiments show that SCODEL consistently improves three modular EL models (ReFinED, GSM-EL, and BLINK): SCODEL x BLINK achieves the highest Hit@1 on seen concepts (88.33%), while SCODEL x GSM-EL achieves the highest Hit@1 on unseen concepts (83.15%), outperforming the strongest large language model (LLM) based EL baseline in each setting. Experiments on a biomedical ontology benchmark further demonstrate that SCODEL generalises beyond the food domain. Finally, we use SCODEL to ground food mentions at scale and construct an ontology-grounded recipe knowledge graph, demonstrating its utility for ontology-aware recipe retrieval and corpus-level food analysis.

infographic.key_insight: SCODEL improves food entity linking by giving contextual recipe mentions and matching ontology concepts shared canonical definitions.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach may support biomedical terminology linking, but this study does not establish clinical utility or patient benefit.
method: Use shared ontology-oriented definitions as a semantic normalisation layer.
Augment ReFinED, GSM-EL and BLINK without introducing a new linking architecture.
Link recipe food mentions to build an ontology-grounded knowledge graph.
infographic.evidence_signal: On the new ReciLinkD benchmark, SCODEL × BLINK reached 88.33% Hit@1 for seen concepts and SCODEL × GSM-EL reached 83.15% for unseen concepts; a biomedical ontology benchmark also showed generalisation.
infographic.watch_item: Clinical deployment would require task-specific validation; the abstract does not report biomedical benchmark details or clinical outcomes.
infographic.paper_title: SCODEL: Shared Canonical Ontology Definitions for Food Entity Linking and Ontology-Grounded Recipe Knowledge Graphs

title: Auto-MD-bench: Evaluating Autoresearch Agents for Real-World Medical Tasks
authors: Shenqi Zhou, Qiran Zou, Wenhao Zhao, Zhenyu Liao, Dianbo Liu
abstract: Autonomous agents are increasingly capable of developing machine learning (ML) models end to end. In medical practice, however, strong performance on the target metric does not fully characterize how good the models are in real-world use cases. For example, medical ML models should also provide well-calibrated risk estimates and remain robust across patient populations. Yet autonomous model development is typically guided by task objectives that emphasize simple predictive discrimination (e.g. AUROC). This raises a key question: are these objectives sufficient to guide agents toward models that meet the broader requirements of real-world medical use? In this study, we introduce Auto-MD-bench, a benchmark of 15 real-world medical tasks from 10 clinical datasets, spanning survival analysis, classification and sequential prediction, with external validation across cohorts, hospitals and time periods. We evaluate four agents: AIDE, AI Scientist v2, Codex, and Autoresearch. The strongest agents achieve competitive primary scores, yet their predicted risks are less calibrated than those of the simple baseline models, which could lead to severe medical accidents. Moreover, models with nearly identical primary scores can exhibit markedly different calibration, while performance varies substantially across population shifts. These findings show that primary task performance alone is insufficient to assess autonomous clinical modeling and multiple different metrics widely used in healthcare practice need to be taken into consideration.

infographic.key_insight: Strong primary prediction scores can mask poor risk calibration and variable performance across patient populations in agent-developed medical ML models.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Evaluating medical ML for real-world use requires assessing risk calibration and robustness across populations, not just predictive discrimination.
method: Introduced Auto-MD-bench with survival analysis, classification, and sequential prediction tasks.
Evaluated AIDE, AI Scientist v2, Codex, and Autoresearch against simple baseline models.
Assessed primary scores, risk calibration, and performance under population shifts.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 15 tasks from 10 clinical datasets, with external validation across cohorts, hospitals, and time periods, the strongest agents achieved competitive primary scores but poorer calibration than simple baselines.
infographic.watch_item: Benchmark performance does not establish clinical safety; calibration and robustness require validation in intended deployment settings.
infographic.paper_title: Auto-MD-bench: Evaluating Autoresearch Agents for Real-World Medical Tasks

title: ECG for laboratory values:A comprehensive physiological and technical analysis
authors: Walentin Palanchuk
abstract: Laboratory measurements are essential for clinical decision making but typically require invasive blood sampling. Recent research suggests that ECG recordings may contain information beyond cardiac rhythm and provide information related to laboratory values. This thesis investigates NT-proBNP prediction from ECG recordings and patient metadata using a multimodal deep learning framework, while considering the physiological plausibility of ECG-based prediction. It also compares a 1-lead configuration using lead II with the corresponding 12-lead configuration. Additional experiments on glucose, hemoglobin, and potassium are presented in the appendix. Regression, binary classification, and three-class classification experiments were conducted using MIMIC-IV, with the three-class task based on clinically established thresholds. The 12-lead configuration consistently achieved better performance. Regression reached a mean absolute error of 534.98 pg/mL for 1-lead and 514.27 pg/mL for 12-lead. Binary classification achieved AUROCs of 0.849 and 0.876, respectively, while three-class classification achieved macro-averaged AUROCs of 0.738 and 0.752. The results indicate that precise NT-proBNP regression remains challenging, whereas broader concentration ranges can be classified more effectively. The findings are consistent with the physiological hypothesis that ECG characteristics and NT-proBNP concentrations reflect shared cardiovascular processes. ECG-based NT-proBNP prediction may therefore provide complementary information, particularly for classifying broader concentration ranges. However, laboratory measurements remain necessary, and validation on independent datasets is required.

infographic.key_insight: ECG and patient metadata supported classification of broad NT-proBNP concentration ranges, with 12-lead ECG outperforming lead II alone, while precise concentration prediction remained challenging.
infographic.clinical_relevance: ECG-based NT-proBNP estimates may offer complementary information about cardiovascular processes but cannot replace laboratory measurements.
method: Multimodal deep learning combined ECG recordings with patient metadata.
Compared lead II alone with 12-lead ECG using MIMIC-IV data.
Evaluated regression, binary classification, and three-class classification using clinically established thresholds.
infographic.evidence_signal: For 1-lead versus 12-lead ECG, regression MAE was 534.98 versus 514.27 pg/mL, binary AUROC was 0.849 versus 0.876, and three-class macro-AUROC was 0.738 versus 0.752.
infographic.watch_item: Independent-dataset validation is needed before considering clinical implementation.
infographic.paper_title: ECG for laboratory values:A comprehensive physiological and technical analysis

title: Convergent Performance, Divergent Mechanisms in LoRA-Adapted Vision Foundation Models for Brain MRI
authors: Cecilia Diana-Albelda, Fiona Kekwick, Raghav Mehta, Aleksandra Kulbaka, Paul M. Matthews, Jesus Bescos
abstract: Adapting Vision Foundation Models (VFMs) to medical imaging via LoRA has become standard practice, yet model selection is guided almost entirely by downstream task metrics, treating backbones with similar performance as interchangeable. We investigate whether equal performance implies equal internal representational shift. We analyse four ViT-B/16 backbones, DINOv3, SigLIP2, MerMED-FM, and BiomedCLIP, pre-trained with different objectives (self-distillation vs. contrastive vision-language) and on different data domains (natural vs. medical images). We adapt each to brain tumour segmentation and evaluate on six datasets covering both segmentation and Alzheimer's disease classification. Using attention divergence, weight-change analysis, and activation patching, we find that the four models converge to similar segmentation performance (mean Dice 78-81%) through markedly different internal dynamics, yet diverge in cross-task transfer: segmentation adaptation improves Alzheimer's disease classification for DINOv3 but degrades it for the other three backbones. We reveal a dissociation between modification magnitude and causal importance: the most heavily modified layers are not the causally relevant ones, with early-to-mid layers identified as sufficient for segmentation recovery. Restricting LoRA to these layers matches or approaches full-layer segmentation while reducing classification degradation in the three affected backbones, providing a mechanistically grounded strategy that is more parameter-efficient and more robust than standard full-layer adaptation.

infographic.key_insight: Four vision backbones reached similar brain tumour segmentation performance through different internal changes, showing that comparable task scores can mask differences in cross-task transfer.
infographic.clinical_relevance: For medical imaging research, backbone and adaptation-layer selection may help preserve performance across tasks rather than optimise segmentation alone.
method: LoRA-adapted DINOv3, SigLIP2, MerMED-FM and BiomedCLIP for brain tumour segmentation.
Probed internal changes using attention divergence, weight-change analysis and activation patching.
Restricted LoRA to causally relevant early-to-mid layers and compared with full-layer adaptation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across six datasets covering segmentation and Alzheimer's disease classification, mean segmentation Dice was 78–81%; adaptation improved classification for DINOv3 but degraded it for the other three backbones.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish prospective clinical performance or whether the layer-selection strategy generalises beyond the studied backbones and tasks.
infographic.paper_title: Convergent Performance, Divergent Mechanisms in LoRA-Adapted Vision Foundation Models for Brain MRI

title: TIM: Temporal Decoupling with Iterative Mutual-Refinement Model for Longitudinal Radiology Report Generation
authors: Yiheng Dong, Yi Lin, Shilong Huang, Xiyan Yang, Xin Yang
abstract: Automatic radiology report generation (RRG) aims to translate medical images into diagnostic text, reducing radiologists' workload and standardizing clinical documentation. Nonetheless, existing approaches mainly focus on single-timepoint analysis and fail to capture temporal disease evolution across longitudinal examinations. While recent longitudinal RRG (LRRG) approaches incorporate historical data, they often combine images from different time points within a single representation space, leading to blurred semantics and inconsistent temporal reasoning. In this work, we propose a Temporal Decoupling with Iterative Mutual-Refinement Model (TIM), a two-stage framework that explicitly decouples spatial pathology from temporal progression and iteratively refines reports through mutual feedback. Stage I performs temporal-decoupled representation learning, separating temporal evolution patterns from disease-specific features and generating radiology reports for both prior and current studies. Stage II introduces a mutual report refinement mechanism that identifies diagnostic inconsistencies within prior reports and iteratively rectifies both prior and current reports through error-sensitive feedback. Experiments on the Longitudinal-MIMIC dataset demonstrate that TIM surpasses existing single-image and longitudinal baselines, achieving new state-of-the-art performance across both language and clinical metrics. Code is available at https://github.com/yihengd/TIM.

infographic.key_insight: TIM separates disease-specific image features from temporal changes, then iteratively refines prior and current radiology reports to improve longitudinal consistency.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could help radiologists document changes across examinations, but clinical benefit and safety remain unestablished.
method: Decouple spatial pathology features from temporal evolution patterns.
Generate reports for both prior and current studies.
Use error-sensitive mutual feedback to iteratively refine both reports.
infographic.evidence_signal: On Longitudinal-MIMIC, TIM reportedly outperformed single-image and longitudinal baselines across language and clinical metrics; the abstract provides no numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Revising prior reports requires safeguards to preserve the original clinical record and prevent incorrect retrospective changes.
infographic.paper_title: TIM: Temporal Decoupling with Iterative Mutual-Refinement Model for Longitudinal Radiology Report Generation
